screens.title: Integrating Postfix with Dovecot for Local Mail Delivery
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on the single, critical step that completes your mail server: telling Postfix to hand local mail to Dovecot for final delivery. You will learn why the mailbox_command exists, how Dovecot’s deliver or dovecot-lda performs local delivery, and how Postfix parameters like mydestination and virtual_alias_maps affect whether mail is handed off. We’ll walk through the minimal changes to /etc/dovecot/conf. d/15-lda. conf and /etc/postfix/main. cf, show how to test delivery end-to-end, and prepare you to diagnose common errors such as incorrect command paths or permission problems. There is also an introduction to virtual users and aliases so you can scale beyond system accounts. By the end you’ll be able to send a test message, confirm a new file in Maildir, and read the Postfix log entries that prove delivery used Dovecot’s LDA. Keep in mind small differences exist across distributions; we’ll show the canonical examples and the checks you should run to adapt the commands safely to your system.

Integrating Postfix with Dovecot

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your work on integrating Postfix and Dovecot so you can deliver mail reliably to user mailboxes. First, you will configure Postfix to hand off local mail delivery to Dovecot’s LDA by setting mailbox_command correctly and ensuring mydestination includes the domains you plan to host. Practically, this matters because a correct handoff prevents message loss and keeps IMAP/POP retrieval consistent. Second, you will understand virtual users and domains at a conceptual level: why virtual accounts let you host many addresses without system accounts, and how Postfix and Dovecot cooperate when virtual mailboxes are used. You’ll see the difference between aliases and virtual mailboxes. Third and fourth objectives cover virtual_alias_maps for aliasing and forwarding, and common troubleshooting patterns. For aliasing, you will create a /etc/postfix/virtual file, convert it with postmap, and reload Postfix. For troubleshooting you will learn to inspect Postfix and Dovecot logs and check Maildir files and permissions. Each objective includes a small verification milestone so you can confirm competency as you go.

screens.title: Dovecot’s Local Delivery Agent (LDA)
screens.narratorSegment: The Local Delivery Agent, or LDA, is the program that actually places mail into a user's mailbox. In our chapter the indispensable LDA is provided by Dovecot — called either deliver or dovecot-lda depending on packaging. Its job is simple and crucial: accept a message handed to it by the MTA and write that message into whatever mailbox format you use, commonly Maildir. A correct LDA understands mailbox locations, enforces permissions, and preserves delivery metadata. A concrete example: when Postfix invokes "/usr/lib/dovecot/deliver -c /etc/dovecot/dovecot. conf -d $USER" the LDA reads Dovecot settings, resolves the user's mail_location like maildir:~/Maildir or maildir:/var/vmail/%d/%n/Maildir for virtual users, and creates a new file in Maildir/new. A common misconception is that the MTA itself writes mail files; in integrated setups the MTA delegates that task to the MDA, and mismatch between MTA delivery method and MDA mailbox format causes message loss or unreadable mail. Key takeaway: ensure the LDA binary exists, matches your Dovecot config, and has appropriate filesystem permissions so Postfix can execute it safely. Dovecot’s Local Delivery Agent (LDA) means dovecot’s lda is responsible for writing received messages into the correct mailbox format and location.. In practical terms, what the lda does and why postfix calls it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: LDA role
keyIdea.text: Dovecot’s LDA is responsible for writing received messages into the correct mailbox format and location.

content.html:
Core Concept › Dovecot LDA
What the LDA does
The LDA writes incoming messages into Maildir or a virtual mailbox path using Dovecot configuration.
Responsibilities
  • Resolve the user's mail_location from Dovecot configuration.
  • Create a new message file in Maildir/new with appropriate metadata.
  • Preserve sender and delivery flags when invoked with the right arguments.
  • Handle virtual mailbox paths for non-system users when configured.
Analogy
Think of the LDA as the mail carrier who puts letters into the correct mailbox — the MTA hands them to the carrier.
Common mistake
Pointing Postfix at a non-existent or wrong-path binary leads to delivery failures.
Example LDA configuration
# /etc/dovecot/conf.d/15-lda.conf
protocol lda {
  # For system users: maildir:~/Maildir
  # For virtual users: mail_location = maildir:/var/vmail/%d/%n/Maildir
  # user = vmail
}
Check
Confirm the LDA binary exists and Dovecot's mail_location matches how you want to store mail.
Key Takeaway

The LDA must align with Dovecot's mail_location; mismatch or missing binary is a primary cause of delivery failure.

screens.title: Configuring Postfix to Use Dovecot’s LDA
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring Postfix to hand off local mail to Dovecot is done by setting mailbox_command in /etc/postfix/main. cf and ensuring Postfix considers a domain local with mydestination. The mailbox_command should call the exact path to dovecot-lda or deliver and pass the recipient so the LDA can resolve the mailbox. A canonical example is mailbox_command = /usr/lib/dovecot/deliver -c /etc/dovecot/dovecot. conf -d $USER. Some systems supply dovecot-lda with different flags, such as -f for sender and -a for recipient; the chapter shows an RHEL/CentOS example using dovecot-dovecot-lda with -f and -a. After editing main. cf, reload Postfix to apply the change. A common misconception is to set mailbox_command but forget to include the domain in mydestination; if Postfix doesn't treat mail as local, it will not invoke mailbox_command. So verify mydestination contains $mydomain or your hosted domains. Finally, remember to check the binary path with which dovecot-lda or find before you commit the change; a wrong path stops delivery entirely. This screen includes a code panel and step checklist to guide your edit. In practical terms, set mailbox_command and ensure mydestination is correct. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. keyIdea.title: Set mailbox_command
keyIdea.text: Point mailbox_command at the system's dovecot-lda/deliver binary and make sure mydestination lists local domains.

content.html:
Process Flow › Configure mailbox_command
Edit /etc/postfix/main.cf
Add or replace mailbox_command and confirm mydestination lists local domains so Postfix invokes the LDA.
# /etc/postfix/main.cf
# Set the command for local mail delivery
mailbox_command = /usr/lib/dovecot/deliver -c /etc/dovecot/dovecot.conf -d $USER

# Ensure Postfix knows which domains are local
mydestination = $myhostname, localhost.$mydomain, localhost, $mydomain
  • Find the correct path with which dovecot-lda or which deliver.
  • Use the binary and flags appropriate for your distro; examples vary.
  • Reload Postfix after edits: sudo systemctl reload postfix.
Checklist & Examples
Example (RHEL/CentOS)
mailbox_command = /usr/libexec/dovecot/dovecot-lda -f "\"$SENDER\"" -a "\"$RECIPIENT\""
Misconception
Setting mailbox_command is necessary but not sufficient—Postfix must also treat the domain as local via mydestination.
Pro Tip
Test the binary directly as the postfix user to confirm it runs and can write to the Maildir location.
Key Takeaway

A correct mailbox_command path and a proper mydestination setting ensure Postfix invokes Dovecot’s LDA for local delivery.

screens.title: Testing Local Delivery End-to-End
screens.narratorSegment: Testing your integration proves your configuration works and gives you quick indicators for troubleshooting. Begin by reloading Postfix so your mailbox_command takes effect. Then send a simple test message from the server to a system user: use the echo pipe with the mail command as shown in the chapter. This writes a message into Postfix’s pickup queue which Postfix should hand to the LDA. After sending, list the recipient's Maildir/new directory; you should see a new file representing the message. If not, check Postfix logs — journalctl -u postfix or /var/log/maillog for a delivery line that mentions delivered via dovecot-lda or deliver. A concrete example: echo "This is a test message for local delivery." | mail -s "Local Delivery Test" mailuser1@your_domain. com and then ls -la /home/mailuser1/Maildir/new/. If logs show unknown user errors, confirm the username resolves to a system account or that Postfix is configured to use virtual mailboxes. A common misconception is assuming an MUA will immediately display messages without checking the filesystem; the Maildir file is the canonical proof of delivery. End the check by confirming Dovecot can list or serve that mailbox over IMAP if needed.

keyIdea.title: Test steps
keyIdea.text: Send a test email from the server, check Maildir/new for a file, and review Postfix logs for a dovecot-lda delivery entry.

content.html:
Verification › Testing Local Delivery
Run these steps
  1. Reload Postfix: sudo systemctl reload postfix
  2. Send a test message from the host: echo "This is a test message for local delivery." | mail -s "Local Delivery Test" mailuser1@your_domain.com
  3. Check Maildir contents: ls -la /home/mailuser1/Maildir/new/
  4. Inspect Postfix logs for delivery: check /var/log/maillog or journalctl -u postfix for "delivered via dovecot" lines.
Example output
You should see a new file in Maildir/new and a Postfix log entry indicating delivery via dovecot-lda or deliver.
Troubleshooting checklist
If Maildir is empty
Confirm mailbox_command path and arguments. Check permissions on the Maildir and parent directories.
If logs show unknown user
Verify Postfix user lookup: is the recipient a system user or must you configure virtual mailboxes and userdb/passdb in Dovecot?
Common mistake
Testing from an external MUA without checking Maildir can mask delivery failures; always verify the file and logs.
Key Takeaway

Use a quick send-and-check loop: send a message, look for Maildir/new, then read logs to confirm dovecot-lda delivery.

screens.title: Virtual Users and Mailboxes — Introduction
screens.narratorSegment: Virtual users let you host many mailboxes without creating corresponding system accounts for each address. Instead of mapping mailboxes to /home/systemuser, Postfix and Dovecot use separate maps or databases to resolve a recipient to a mailbox path like /var/vmail/domain/user/Maildir. This approach improves scalability and security for hosting multiple domains. A concrete example: info@your_domain. com can be a virtual user stored under /var/vmail/your_domain/info/Maildir while the system has no user named info. To make this work, Postfix must consult virtual_mailbox_maps or similar lookup sources to know where to hand mail, and Dovecot must have userdb/passdb entries that resolve virtual usernames to the correct mail_location and ownership, often using a single system user such as vmail to own mailbox files. A common misconception is assuming system user delivery and virtual delivery use the same defaults; they do not. Virtual setups require explicit mapping in Postfix and matching userdb configuration in Dovecot so the LDA can place the message into the virtual mailbox path. Virtual Users and Mailboxes — Introduction means virtual users decouple mail identities from system accounts, enabling many domains and mailboxes managed via maps or databases.. In practical terms, why virtual users matter for multi-domain hosting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Virtual users
keyIdea.text: Virtual users decouple mail identities from system accounts, enabling many domains and mailboxes managed via maps or databases.

content.html:
Definition › Virtual Users & Mailboxes
What is a virtual user?
A mail identity that does not require a corresponding system account; mailboxes stored in a separate vmail hierarchy.
Example path
mail_location = maildir:/var/vmail/%d/%n/Maildir resolves domain and user into a directory.
  • Postfix uses virtual_mailbox_maps and virtual_mailbox_domains to map recipients to mailboxes.
  • Dovecot needs userdb/passdb entries or an SQL/LDAP lookup for virtual users.
  • Files are often owned by a dedicated mail user such as vmail to centralize permissions.
Migration note
When moving from system to virtual users, update Postfix maps and Dovecot userdb so delivery paths change without breaking client access.
Common mistake
Forgetting to align Postfix virtual maps with Dovecot userdb results in unknown user or permission errors.
Practical tip
Use a single mail owner UID/GID for virtual maildirs and ensure both Postfix and Dovecot can access them.
Key Takeaway

Virtual users allow hosting many domains without system accounts but require explicit mapping in both Postfix and Dovecot.

screens.title: System Users vs Virtual Users
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing system accounts or virtual users affects how you manage mail and scale domains. System users map mailboxes to Linux accounts and home directories — Maildir:~/Maildir is typical. This is simple and works well for a small set of users. Virtual users decouple email identities from system accounts and store mail under a shared directory hierarchy such as /var/vmail/%d/%n/Maildir. This is essential when hosting many domains or when you do not want to create hundreds of system accounts. A concrete example: a small team can use system users with home directories, while an ISP-like service needs virtual users. A common misconception is that virtual users are inherently insecure; they are not, but they require deliberate userdb/passdb and ownership conventions. Practically, Postfix configuration differs: system delivery can rely on mailbox_command with $USER, whereas virtual delivery often needs virtual_mailbox_maps and Dovecot userdb entries. When you inspect logs and see unknown user errors, check whether Postfix expects a system user or a virtual mapping — that mismatch is a frequent source of failure. System Users vs Virtual Users means system users are simpler for small deployments; virtual users scale for multi-domain hosting but require extra mapping configuration.. In practical terms, understand differences and when to choose each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › System vs Virtual Users
System Users
Maildir in user home directories. Easier to set up for a handful of accounts.
  • Uses system account names; $USER works for mailbox_command.
  • Simpler authentication if accounts already exist on the system.
  • Less flexible for hosting many domains.
When to use
Small teams, single domain, or when system accounts are already managed centrally.
Virtual Users
Separate mapping from system accounts, suitable for many domains and mailboxes.
  • Requires virtual_mailbox_maps and userdb/passdb in Dovecot.
  • Mail stored under centralized path like /var/vmail/%d/%n/Maildir.
  • Scales without creating system users.
When to use
Multi-domain hosting, service providers, or when you want a dedicated mail owner user.
Key Takeaway

Pick system users for simplicity and virtual users for scale; ensure Postfix and Dovecot mappings match your choice to avoid delivery errors.

screens.title: virtual_alias_maps and Alias Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Postfix uses virtual_alias_maps to implement aliases and forwarding rules. You declare virtual_alias_maps in /etc/postfix/main. cf pointing to a lookup table such as hash:/etc/postfix/virtual. The text file lists alias mappings like info@your_domain. com mailuser1 or sales@your_domain. com external_email@another. com. After editing the file you run postmap /etc/postfix/virtual to build the hash database Postfix uses at runtime, then reload Postfix. A concrete example in the chapter shows creating /etc/postfix/virtual with internal and external targets, then running postmap and systemctl reload postfix. This workflow is powerful because aliases can forward to local users, virtual users, or external addresses. A common misconception is forgetting to run postmap — Postfix will not read the updated text file until the DB is built. When designing alias rules remember the lookup order and ensure aliases do not create forwarding loops. keyIdea.title: Alias mapping
keyIdea.text: Use virtual_alias_maps with a hashed database; always run postmap and reload Postfix after editing the alias file.

content.html:
Process › virtual_alias_maps
Alias file and postmap
# /etc/postfix/main.cf
virtual_alias_maps = hash:/etc/postfix/virtual

# /etc/postfix/virtual
info@your_domain.com mailuser1
sales@your_domain.com external_email@another.com
  • After editing: sudo postmap /etc/postfix/virtual
  • Then: sudo systemctl reload postfix
  • Postfix consults the hashed DB at delivery time to expand aliases.
Architecture note
On receipt, Postfix looks up the recipient in virtual_alias_maps; if an alias is found it rewrites the envelope recipient and routes accordingly.
Misconception
Editing the text file alone is not enough. You must run postmap to create the hashed DB that Postfix uses.
Key Takeaway

virtual_alias_maps plus postmap is the correct workflow for managing aliases and forwarding in Postfix.

screens.title: Example Edits: 15-lda.conf and main.cf
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through the two files you edit when integrating Postfix and Dovecot: Dovecot's 15-lda. conf and Postfix's main. cf. In 15-lda. conf you enable the protocol lda block and set mail_location appropriately. For system users the default mail_location = maildir:~/Maildir may already work. For virtual users you might set mail_location = maildir:/var/vmail/%d/%n/Maildir and configure user = vmail to run delivery under a dedicated account. In main. cf you add mailbox_command pointing to the exact LDA binary and use -c to pass the dovecot config and -d or -a to pass the recipient. Before reloading Postfix, run which dovecot-lda or find to confirm the binary path and ensure the postfix user has execute permissions and access to the mailbox directories. If you are on RHEL or CentOS, the chapter notes an example path of /usr/libexec/dovecot/dovecot-lda and flags like -f and -a may be used. After edits, reload Postfix and send a test message. If something fails, the next screen covers targeted troubleshooting steps. keyIdea.text: Confirm LDA binary path and Dovecot mail_location before reloading Postfix to avoid service interruptions.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › 15-lda.conf & main.cf
15-lda.conf (Dovecot)
# /etc/dovecot/conf.d/15-lda.conf
protocol lda {
  # For system users
  # mail_location = maildir:~/Maildir

  # For virtual users
  # mail_location = maildir:/var/vmail/%d/%n/Maildir
  # user = vmail
}
Enable protocol lda and set mail_location to match your mailbox layout. If using virtual mailboxes, ensure a consistent owner and permissions.
main.cf (Postfix)
# /etc/postfix/main.cf
mailbox_command = /usr/lib/dovecot/deliver -c /etc/dovecot/dovecot.conf -d $USER
mydestination = $myhostname, localhost.$mydomain, localhost, $mydomain
Confirm the exact path and flags for your distribution, then reload Postfix and run a delivery test.
Sanity check
Run which dovecot-lda or which deliver to confirm the executable path.
Permissions
Ensure the Postfix process can execute the LDA and the LDA user can write to the mailbox dirs.
If you see errors
Check both Postfix and Dovecot logs for failures before changing configuration further.

screens.title: Common Integration Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: When integrating Postfix and Dovecot you will frequently encounter a small set of issues. First, an incorrect mailbox_command path means Postfix cannot execute the LDA. Fix: run which dovecot-lda or which deliver, correct the path in main. cf, and reload Postfix. Second, permission problems — if the LDA cannot write to Maildir due to ownership or mode, deliveries fail. Fix: set ownership to the expected user (system account or vmail) and ensure directories are writable. Third, mydestination not including your domain prevents Postfix from treating mail as local and therefore it will not call mailbox_command. Fix: add the domain to mydestination. Fourth, Dovecot LDA disabled or misconfigured in 15-lda. conf, leaving mail_location wrong for virtual users. Fix: enable the lda protocol and set mail_location to the virtual path. For each issue this screen gives the log lines or filesystem checks to run and the minimal commands to remediate. A common misconception is that restarting services always helps; first inspect logs to identify which of the four root causes applies so you fix the specific fault. content.html:
Troubleshooting › Common mistakes
Issue → How to check → Fix
Incorrect mailbox_command path
Check with: which dovecot-lda. Fix main.cf and reload Postfix.
Permission problems
Check Maildir ownership and modes: ls -la /home/mailuser/Maildir. Fix ownership and permissions so LDA can write.
mydestination missing domain
Check main.cf. If Postfix doesn't consider the domain local, mailbox_command won't be invoked. Add domain to mydestination.
Dovecot LDA disabled or misconfigured
Inspect /etc/dovecot/conf.d/15-lda.conf and ensure mail_location lines are correct for system or virtual users.
Log indicators and commands
  • Postfix delivery entries: look for "status=sent (delivered via dovecot-lda)".
  • Unknown user errors suggest a mismatch between Postfix and Dovecot user lookup.
  • Use journalctl -u postfix -n 50 or tail of maillog to get recent hints.
Practical tip
Reproduce the error with a test message and capture logs immediately after to see the precise failure mode before changing config widely.
Key Takeaway

Check binary paths, permissions, domain settings, and Dovecot LDA configuration in that order to quickly resolve delivery issues.

Hands-on Activity › Integrate Postfix & Dovecot
Step-by-step checklist
  1. Verify /etc/dovecot/conf.d/15-lda.conf and mail_location.
  2. Set mailbox_command in /etc/postfix/main.cf to the correct binary.
  3. Ensure your domain is in mydestination and reload Postfix.
  4. Send a test message and check Maildir/new for the new file.
  5. For aliases, edit /etc/postfix/virtual, run sudo postmap /etc/postfix/virtual, and reload Postfix.
Verification & expected checks
  • Maildir contains a new file: ls -la /home/mailuser1/Maildir/new/.
  • Postfix logs show delivery via dovecot-lda: look for "delivered via dovecot-lda" lines.
  • For aliased mail, confirm forwarding targets receive messages after postmap and reload.
Note
If multiple issues appear, fix the path and permissions first, then address mapping errors.
Key Takeaway

Follow the checklist in order: LDA config, mailbox_command, reload, test, and then alias mapping with postmap to ensure clean integration.

screens.title: Assessment: Diagnose a Delivery Failure
screens.narratorSegment: The assessment from the chapter asks you to diagnose a delivery problem where Postfix accepts mail but messages do not appear in Dovecot-managed mailboxes, and logs show unknown user or delivery failures. The most likely misconfigured parameter is mailbox_command, because that setting instructs Postfix to call the external program that places mail into user mailboxes. To evaluate, perform these checks: verify mailbox_command exists and points to the correct LDA binary; confirm mydestination lists the domain; check Dovecot’s LDA configuration for mail_location and protocol lda; inspect Maildir permissions and ownership; and read Postfix logs for messages mentioning dovecot-lda or deliver. A concrete example: if Postfix logs show "unknown user: mailuser" but the system account exists, mailbox_command might be missing or wrongly configured so Postfix falls back to a default delivery mechanism that doesn't match Dovecot. content.html:
Assessment › Diagnose Delivery Failure
Scenario
Postfix accepts mail but Maildir remains empty; logs show user-related errors.
Stepwise diagnosis
  1. Check mailbox_command in main.cf for correct path and args.
  2. Inspect /var/log/maillog or journalctl -u postfix for dovecot delivery lines.
  3. Verify Dovecot LDA configuration and mail_location.
  4. Confirm mailbox ownership and permissions.
Correct answer rationale
The mailbox_command parameter instructs Postfix to use an external program, and if it is missing or wrong Postfix will not hand mail to Dovecot’s LDA. That leads to mismatches between what Postfix does and where Dovecot expects mail.
Misconception
Other parameters like mynetworks or inet_interfaces control network and listener behavior but not the MTA→MDA handoff.
Key Takeaway

When delivery fails while Postfix accepts mail, mailbox_command is the primary Postfix setting to verify; follow logs and mailbox checks to confirm.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the essential concepts you should retain. First, the Local Delivery Agent is the program that writes mail into the mailbox; Dovecot provides deliver or dovecot-lda and must be aligned with Dovecot's mail_location. Second, mailbox_command is the Postfix parameter that tells Postfix which external program to run for local delivery; a wrong path or missing flags will prevent correct handoff. Third, virtual users and virtual domains let you host many mailboxes without system accounts; this requires matching Postfix maps and Dovecot userdb/passdb entries. As a reminder, the alias workflow uses virtual_alias_maps plus postmap to create the hashed database Postfix reads at runtime. Finally, when deliveries fail, the first checks are mailbox_command path, permissions on Maildirs, mydestination domain configuration, and Dovecot’s LDA settings. Keep these core ideas in mind as a checklist when you configure or troubleshoot MTA–MDA integrations.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on the single, critical step that completes your mail server: telling Postfix to hand local mail to Dovecot for final delivery. You will learn why the mailbox_command exists, how Dovecot’s deliver or dovecot-lda performs local delivery, and how Postfix parameters like mydestination and virtual_alias_maps affect whether mail is handed off. We’ll walk through the minimal changes to /etc/dovecot/conf. d/15-lda. conf and /etc/postfix/main. cf, show how to test delivery end-to-end, and prepare you to diagnose common errors such as incorrect command paths or permission problems. There is also an introduction to virtual users and aliases so you can scale beyond system accounts. By the end you’ll be able to send a test message, confirm a new file in Maildir, and read the Postfix log entries that prove delivery used Dovecot’s LDA. Keep in mind small differences exist across distributions; we’ll show the canonical examples and the checks you should run to adapt the commands safely to your system.

These objectives focus your work on integrating Postfix and Dovecot so you can deliver mail reliably to user mailboxes. First, you will configure Postfix to hand off local mail delivery to Dovecot’s LDA by setting mailbox_command correctly and ensuring mydestination includes the domains you plan to host. Practically, this matters because a correct handoff prevents message loss and keeps IMAP/POP retrieval consistent. Second, you will understand virtual users and domains at a conceptual level: why virtual accounts let you host many addresses without system accounts, and how Postfix and Dovecot cooperate when virtual mailboxes are used. You’ll see the difference between aliases and virtual mailboxes. Third and fourth objectives cover virtual_alias_maps for aliasing and forwarding, and common troubleshooting patterns. For aliasing, you will create a /etc/postfix/virtual file, convert it with postmap, and reload Postfix. For troubleshooting you will learn to inspect Postfix and Dovecot logs and check Maildir files and permissions. Each objective includes a small verification milestone so you can confirm competency as you go.

This second objectives screen describes the hands-on tasks you will perform and how to verify success. You will check Dovecot’s LDA configuration file 15-lda. conf to ensure the protocol lda block is enabled and the mail_location points to Maildir or the virtual path used by your setup. For Postfix, you will set mailbox_command to the exact path for dovecot-lda or deliver and include proper arguments like -f for sender and -a or -d for recipient where required. After configuration you will reload Postfix and send a test message from the server to the system user or virtual user. Verification includes looking for a new message file inside Maildir/new and reading Postfix logs for lines that show delivery via dovecot-lda or deliver. Finally, you will create a simple /etc/postfix/virtual alias file, run postmap on it, reload Postfix, and confirm forwarding behavior. Each validation step proves the configuration and makes debugging straightforward.

The Local Delivery Agent, or LDA, is the program that actually places mail into a user's mailbox. In our chapter the indispensable LDA is provided by Dovecot — called either deliver or dovecot-lda depending on packaging. Its job is simple and crucial: accept a message handed to it by the MTA and write that message into whatever mailbox format you use, commonly Maildir. A correct LDA understands mailbox locations, enforces permissions, and preserves delivery metadata. A concrete example: when Postfix invokes "/usr/lib/dovecot/deliver -c /etc/dovecot/dovecot. conf -d $USER" the LDA reads Dovecot settings, resolves the user's mail_location like maildir:~/Maildir or maildir:/var/vmail/%d/%n/Maildir for virtual users, and creates a new file in Maildir/new. A common misconception is that the MTA itself writes mail files; in integrated setups the MTA delegates that task to the MDA, and mismatch between MTA delivery method and MDA mailbox format causes message loss or unreadable mail. Key takeaway: ensure the LDA binary exists, matches your Dovecot config, and has appropriate filesystem permissions so Postfix can execute it safely. Configuring Postfix to hand off local mail to Dovecot is done by setting mailbox_command in /etc/postfix/main. cf and ensuring Postfix considers a domain local with mydestination. The mailbox_command should call the exact path to dovecot-lda or deliver and pass the recipient so the LDA can resolve the mailbox. A canonical example is mailbox_command = /usr/lib/dovecot/deliver -c /etc/dovecot/dovecot. conf -d $USER. Some systems supply dovecot-lda with different flags, such as -f for sender and -a for recipient; the chapter shows an RHEL/CentOS example using dovecot-dovecot-lda with -f and -a. After editing main. cf, reload Postfix to apply the change. A common misconception is to set mailbox_command but forget to include the domain in mydestination; if Postfix doesn't treat mail as local, it will not invoke mailbox_command. So verify mydestination contains $mydomain or your hosted domains. Virtual users let you host many mailboxes without creating corresponding system accounts for each address. Instead of mapping mailboxes to /home/systemuser, Postfix and Dovecot use separate maps or databases to resolve a recipient to a mailbox path like /var/vmail/domain/user/Maildir. This approach improves scalability and security for hosting multiple domains. A concrete example: info@your_domain. com can be a virtual user stored under /var/vmail/your_domain/info/Maildir while the system has no user named info. To make this work, Postfix must consult virtual_mailbox_maps or similar lookup sources to know where to hand mail, and Dovecot must have userdb/passdb entries that resolve virtual usernames to the correct mail_location and ownership, often using a single system user such as vmail to own mailbox files. A common misconception is assuming system user delivery and virtual delivery use the same defaults; they do not. Virtual setups require explicit mapping in Postfix and matching userdb configuration in Dovecot so the LDA can place the message into the virtual mailbox path. Choosing system accounts or virtual users affects how you manage mail and scale domains. System users map mailboxes to Linux accounts and home directories — Maildir:~/Maildir is typical. This is simple and works well for a small set of users. Virtual users decouple email identities from system accounts and store mail under a shared directory hierarchy such as /var/vmail/%d/%n/Maildir. This is essential when hosting many domains or when you do not want to create hundreds of system accounts. A concrete example: a small team can use system users with home directories, while an ISP-like service needs virtual users. A common misconception is that virtual users are inherently insecure; they are not, but they require deliberate userdb/passdb and ownership conventions. Practically, Postfix configuration differs: system delivery can rely on mailbox_command with $USER, whereas virtual delivery often needs virtual_mailbox_maps and Dovecot userdb entries. When you inspect logs and see unknown user errors, check whether Postfix expects a system user or a virtual mapping — that mismatch is a frequent source of failure. When integrating Postfix and Dovecot you will frequently encounter a small set of issues. First, an incorrect mailbox_command path means Postfix cannot execute the LDA. Fix: run which dovecot-lda or which deliver, correct the path in main. cf, and reload Postfix. Second, permission problems — if the LDA cannot write to Maildir due to ownership or mode, deliveries fail. Fix: set ownership to the expected user (system account or vmail) and ensure directories are writable. Third, mydestination not including your domain prevents Postfix from treating mail as local and therefore it will not call mailbox_command. Fix: add the domain to mydestination. Fourth, Dovecot LDA disabled or misconfigured in 15-lda. conf, leaving mail_location wrong for virtual users. Fix: enable the lda protocol and set mail_location to the virtual path. For each issue this screen gives the log lines or filesystem checks to run and the minimal commands to remediate. These are the essential concepts you should retain. First, the Local Delivery Agent is the program that writes mail into the mailbox; Dovecot provides deliver or dovecot-lda and must be aligned with Dovecot's mail_location. Second, mailbox_command is the Postfix parameter that tells Postfix which external program to run for local delivery; a wrong path or missing flags will prevent correct handoff. Third, virtual users and virtual domains let you host many mailboxes without system accounts; this requires matching Postfix maps and Dovecot userdb/passdb entries. As a reminder, the alias workflow uses virtual_alias_maps plus postmap to create the hashed database Postfix reads at runtime. Finally, when deliveries fail, the first checks are mailbox_command path, permissions on Maildirs, mydestination domain configuration, and Dovecot’s LDA settings. Keep these core ideas in mind as a checklist when you configure or troubleshoot MTA–MDA integrations.
